note: The recurring SHAPES of PSLE Science Booklet B open-ended questions, independent of topic. A student who can name the shape already knows what the mark scheme wants, because each shape rewards a fixed structure. Signposts are the literal words in a stem that reveal the shape. Every trap listed is one examiners report year after year.

universalHeuristics.rule: Marks tell you how many points, not how long to write.
universalHeuristics.detail: One mark, one separate scientific point. A 4 mark question wants four things the examiner can tick, not one thing said four ways. Before writing, count the marks and plan that many points.
universalHeuristics.test: Read your answer back and count the ticks. Fewer ticks than marks means you have not finished.

universalHeuristics.rule: Name the process. Do not describe it.
universalHeuristics.detail: The named term is usually the mark itself. 'The water dried up' describes; 'the water evaporated' names. 'The plant gave out water' describes; 'transpiration' names.
universalHeuristics.test: Underline every verb. If a verb could appear in a conversation about the weather, it probably needs replacing.

universalHeuristics.rule: State the middle, not just the ends.
universalHeuristics.detail: A grade AL3 answer says where it started and where it ended. An AL1 answer puts the mechanism between them. If your answer jumps from cause to result in one step, a mark is missing in the gap.
universalHeuristics.test: Can you insert the word 'so' between every pair of sentences and have it still make sense? If not, a link is missing.

universalHeuristics.detail: Repeating the stem in different words scores nothing. If the question says the bulb goes out, writing 'because the bulb went out' is not an answer.
universalHeuristics.test: Cross out any sentence that a person who had not studied Science could have written from the question alone.

universalHeuristics.rule: If data is given, quote it.
universalHeuristics.detail: A table or graph is not decoration. An inference with no figures in it almost always drops a mark, because the examiner cannot see that you read the data.
universalHeuristics.test: Does at least one number, or one named row, appear in your answer?

universalHeuristics.rule: If two things are named, answer about both.
universalHeuristics.detail: When a stem mentions a metal spoon and a wooden spoon, both are in the mark scheme. Explaining one beautifully leaves half the marks behind.
universalHeuristics.test: Circle every object named in the stem. Each one should appear in your answer.

universalHeuristics.detail: Whenever you compare two setups, they must differ in exactly one thing. If two things differ, the result cannot tell you which one caused it, and saying so is often itself a mark.
universalHeuristics.test: List what is different between the two setups. If the list has more than one item, you have the wrong pair.

universalHeuristics.detail: Heat flows from hotter to colder. Energy is transferred from A to B. Water moves from the roots to the leaves. Direction is frequently a mark on its own, and 'cold moves in' is marked wrong.
universalHeuristics.test: Every transfer in your answer should have a from and a to.

universalHeuristics.rule: Nothing is used up, and nothing is given by nature.
universalHeuristics.detail: Energy is converted, not used up. Plants make food, not energy. Cold does not move. Air is not sucked in. Each of these is a specific error examiners mark wrong even when the idea behind it is close.
universalHeuristics.test: Search your answer for 'used up', 'makes energy', 'the cold', 'sucks'. Each one is probably costing a mark.

universalHeuristics.rule: Finish at the thing the question asked about.
universalHeuristics.detail: An adaptation answer must end at survival. An energy answer must end at the form the energy took. A food chain answer must end at the population asked about. Stopping one step early is the most common near miss.
universalHeuristics.test: Does the last sentence of your answer mention the thing the question named?

signposts.means: Give the cause and the mechanism. A statement of fact is not enough.
Give the sequence by which it happens, step by step.
There is an apparent contradiction and you must address it directly. The words after 'even though' are the trap.
Same as 'even though'. Something looks inconsistent and the answer must resolve it.
Both things in every point. Usually one similarity and one difference.
A comparison, but differences only. Still mention both things in each point.
Quote figures or named rows from the table. An answer with no data in it will drop a mark.
Describe what the graph does, then explain why. Both halves are marked.
State the conclusion and the evidence that supports it. Name the rows you compared.
Answer in the fixed form: as X increases, Y increases or decreases.
Answer in the fixed form: to find out how the changed variable affects the measured variable.
Find the variable that should have been kept the same and was not.

signposts.phrase: suggest how you would find out
signposts.means: Design an experiment: what to change, what to measure, what to keep the same, and what result would prove it.
State the outcome first, then the reason. A prediction with no reason scores half.
A prediction. State what happens and why.
More than one answer may be accepted, but yours must actually work and must come with a reason.
Link the feature to the mechanism, then to survival or purpose.
Choose one, justify with its properties, and say why the others fail.
State what happens, in order. No reasons required, but nothing may be skipped.
One line. No explanation wanted, and adding one wastes time you need elsewhere.

signposts.phrase: give a reason for your answer
signposts.means: The identification alone is not the mark. The deciding evidence is.
Explain the difference, not just describe it.
Your answer must use that named idea. Anything else, however true, is off target.

archetypes.name: The mechanism chain
archetypes.oneLine: Why or how something happens. The single most common shape in Booklet B.
archetypes.alwaysWants: A causal chain: the cause, the named process in the middle, and the effect. The middle link is what separates AL1 from AL3.
skeleton: State the cause, using the situation from the question.
Name the scientific process that the cause sets off.
State the effect that process produces.
If more marks remain, extend the chain or add a second linked cause.
archetypes.trap: Stating A and C and leaving out B. 'The water was in the sun so the puddle disappeared' has the two ends and no mechanism, and scores one mark of two.

worked.stem: Explain why the puddle disappeared after a hot afternoon.
worked.weak: The sun dried up the water.
worked.strong: Water in the puddle gained heat energy from the sun. This caused the water to evaporate, changing from the liquid state into water vapour, which escaped into the air.
worked.whatChanged: Named the process, evaporation, and named what the water gained, heat energy. Those two words are the two marks.

archetypes.name: The apparent contradiction
archetypes.oneLine: Something in the question looks like it should not be true, and you must resolve it.
archetypes.alwaysWants: Direct engagement with the surprising part. The examiner has planted the contradiction on purpose and the mark is for dissolving it.
skeleton: Name the distinction the question is testing, usually two ideas that get confused.
Explain the case as it appears.
Explain why the apparent contradiction is not really one.
archetypes.trap: Ignoring the 'even though' clause and answering only the first half of the sentence. The clause after 'even though' is where the mark sits.

worked.stem: Explain why the bathtub contains more heat energy than the cup, even though its temperature is lower.
worked.weak: The bathtub is bigger so it has more heat.
worked.strong: Temperature is a measure of how hot something is, while heat energy is the total amount of energy contained. The bathtub holds far more water, so even though each part of it is cooler, the total heat energy in the bath is greater.
worked.whatChanged: Separated the two ideas the question deliberately confuses. Without that sentence there is no answer at all.

archetypes.name: The comparison
archetypes.oneLine: Two things set side by side. Usually one similarity and one difference.
recognise: how is X different from Y
archetypes.alwaysWants: Both things mentioned in every point. A comparison written as two separate descriptions is not a comparison.
skeleton: State one way both are the same, naming both.
State one way they differ, naming both and using a linking word such as while or whereas.
If marks remain, add the consequence of the difference.
archetypes.trap: Describing A fully, then describing B fully. Every sentence should contain both, joined by while or whereas.

worked.stem: Compare the properties of a liquid and a gas.
worked.weak: A liquid has a fixed volume. A gas spreads out everywhere.
worked.strong: Both a liquid and a gas have no definite shape and take the shape of their container. However, a liquid has a definite volume while a gas has no definite volume, so a gas fills its container completely whereas a liquid does not.
worked.whatChanged: Every sentence now holds both substances. The similarity was added, and 'while' does the comparing.

archetypes.name: The data inference
archetypes.oneLine: A table of results, and a conclusion to draw from it.
archetypes.alwaysWants: The conclusion, plus the specific comparison that supports it. Name the rows and quote the figures.
skeleton: State the conclusion.
Name the two rows you compared and say that only one factor differs between them.
Quote the figures and say what the difference shows.
If a row seems to contradict you, deal with it. It is there on purpose.
archetypes.trap: Reaching the right conclusion from the wrong pair. If two things differ between the rows you chose, your evidence proves nothing.

worked.stem: Four wet cloths dried in different conditions. What affects the rate of evaporation?
worked.weak: Cloth Z dried fastest, so sun and wind both help.
worked.strong: Comparing Cloth W with Cloth X, where only the air movement differs, the windy cloth dried in 180 minutes against 300, so moving air increases the rate of evaporation.
worked.whatChanged: Z had two differences, so it proves nothing on its own. The W and X pair isolates one factor, and the figures show the size of the effect.

archetypes.name: The relationship statement
archetypes.oneLine: How one variable changes with another. A fixed sentence form.
archetypes.alwaysWants: The set form: as the [changed variable] increases, the [measured variable] increases or decreases.
skeleton: Begin with 'As the'.
Name the changed variable and say increases or decreases.
Name the measured variable and say increases or decreases.
archetypes.trap: Giving one pair of readings instead of the pattern. A relationship describes the whole trend, not a single row.

worked.stem: What is the relationship between the number of turns of wire and the strength of the electromagnet?
worked.weak: 40 turns picked up 8 clips and 20 turns picked up 4.
worked.strong: As the number of turns of wire increases, the strength of the electromagnet increases.
worked.whatChanged: The weak version reports data. The strong version states the pattern, which is what a relationship question asks for.

archetypes.name: The aim of the experiment
archetypes.oneLine: What the experiment was trying to find out. Also a fixed form.
recognise: what was the purpose of the experiment
what was he trying to find out
archetypes.alwaysWants: To find out how the changed variable affects the measured variable. Both variables must be named.
skeleton: Begin with 'To find out how' or 'To find out whether'.
Name the variable that was deliberately changed.
Name the variable that was measured.
archetypes.trap: Describing what was done instead of what was being found out. The aim is a question the experiment answers, not a set of instructions.

worked.stem: State the aim of the experiment in which four dishes of water were kept at different temperatures.
worked.weak: To put water in dishes at different temperatures and see what happens.
worked.strong: To find out how the temperature of the surroundings affects the rate of evaporation of water.
worked.whatChanged: Both variables named, and the sentence now states a purpose rather than a procedure.

archetypes.name: The fair test critique
archetypes.oneLine: An experiment with something wrong with it.
recognise: what is wrong with this experiment
how could the test be improved
archetypes.alwaysWants: The variable that should have been kept the same and was not, plus how to fix it.
skeleton: Name the variable that differs and should not.
Say why that ruins the conclusion: the result could be due to either factor.
State the fix: keep that variable the same and change only the one being tested.
archetypes.trap: Confusing fairness with reliability. Keeping variables the same makes a test fair; repeating it and averaging makes the result reliable. Many questions want both, and they are separate marks.

worked.stem: A student tested wind speed using a shallow dish beside a fan and a tall jar in a still corner.
worked.weak: It is not fair because the containers are different.
worked.strong: Two things were changed at once, the air movement and the shape of the container, so any difference in water lost could be due to either. She should use two identical dishes with the same volume of water and change only whether the fan is on.
worked.whatChanged: Named the consequence, that the result is uninterpretable, and gave the fix. Spotting the flaw is only the first mark.

archetypes.name: The experiment design
recognise: suggest how you would find out
archetypes.alwaysWants: Four things: what to change, what to measure, what to keep the same, and what result would prove the point.
skeleton: Set up two or more identical arrangements.
State the one thing that differs between them.
List what is kept the same.
State what will be measured, as a number that can be recorded.
State what result would support the claim.
archetypes.trap: Omitting the measurement, or omitting the control. 'See which is wetter' is not a measurement. A setup with nothing to compare against proves nothing.

worked.stem: Suggest how the student could test whether saliva breaks down starch.
worked.weak: Add saliva to starch and test it after a while.
worked.strong: Set up two tubes with the same amount of starch solution. Add saliva to one and the same volume of water to the other as a control. Keep both at the same temperature for the same time, then test both for starch. Starch remaining in the water tube but absent from the saliva tube shows the saliva broke it down.
worked.whatChanged: The control tube is the mark most often missed. Without it, nothing has been shown.

archetypes.name: The prediction
archetypes.alwaysWants: The outcome stated first, then the reason. A bare prediction scores at most half.
skeleton: State the outcome plainly in the first sentence.
Give the mechanism that causes it.
If marks remain, state the end point or a limitation.
archetypes.trap: Giving the outcome with no reason, or a reason that restates the change. 'It will be faster because it is hotter' has not explained anything.

worked.stem: Predict which dish will contain less water after four hours.
worked.weak: Dish B, because it is in the sun.
worked.strong: Dish B will contain less water. Dish B receives more heat energy from the sunlight, and the greater the heat energy gained, the higher the rate of evaporation, so more water evaporates in the same time.
worked.whatChanged: The phrase rate of evaporation turns a restatement into a mechanism.

archetypes.name: The suggestion or improvement
archetypes.oneLine: Offer a way to solve, improve or prevent something.
archetypes.alwaysWants: A practical action that would actually work, plus the reason it works. Several answers may be accepted.
skeleton: State the action, specifically enough that someone could carry it out.
Explain the mechanism by which it works.
If the question asks for two suggestions, give two separate reasons as well.
archetypes.trap: Listing actions with no reasons. Suggest questions still carry explanation marks, and two suggestions need two explanations.

worked.stem: Suggest one thing the family could do to make clothes dry faster indoors.
worked.strong: Switch on a fan so air moves over the clothes. Moving air carries away the water vapour near the wet cloth, which increases the rate of evaporation.
worked.whatChanged: The action was already right. The mark was in the mechanism, which the weak answer never gave.

archetypes.name: The feature and its function
archetypes.oneLine: A structure is described and you must say what it does for the organism or object.
archetypes.alwaysWants: Structure, then mechanism, then the benefit. Adaptation answers must end at survival.
skeleton: Name the feature as the question describes it.
State the property it gives, very often surface area.
State what that allows the organism or object to do.
End at survival, or at the purpose the question named.
archetypes.trap: Stopping at the property without reaching the benefit. Also, repeating the stem: 'the spines are small' is given in the question, not an answer.

worked.stem: Explain how the thin spines of a desert plant help it survive.
worked.weak: The spines are small so it does not lose much water.
worked.strong: The spines have a very small surface area, which greatly reduces the amount of water lost from the plant. This allows the plant to conserve water and survive in a desert where there is very little rain.
worked.whatChanged: Named surface area as the property, and ended at survival in that habitat.

archetypes.name: The best choice with justification
archetypes.oneLine: Several options, one is most suitable, say which and why.
archetypes.alwaysWants: The choice, every relevant property linked to the requirement, and usually why the rejected options fail.
skeleton: Name your choice.
Take each property in turn and link it to what the job needs.
Say why each rejected option is unsuitable, naming the property that rules it out.
archetypes.trap: Naming the winner and stopping. When four options are given and the question is worth three marks, the rejections are carrying marks.

worked.stem: Which of four fabrics is most suitable for a raincoat?
worked.weak: Material J, because it is the best one.
worked.strong: Material J. It is waterproof so rain cannot pass through, flexible so it can be worn comfortably, and does not tear easily so it will last. L absorbs water so the wearer would get wet, K is too stiff to wear, and M tears easily.
worked.whatChanged: Each property tied to a requirement of a raincoat, and each rejection tied to the property that disqualifies it.

archetypes.name: The ordered description
archetypes.oneLine: State what happens, in order. No reasons wanted.
archetypes.alwaysWants: Every stage, in the right order, with each one named. Marks are usually one per stage.
skeleton: Work through the stages in order.
Name each stage or process rather than describing it.
Do not skip a stage because it seems obvious; the skipped one is usually the mark.
archetypes.trap: Skipping the middle stage. The pupa in a life cycle, the heart between lungs and muscle, condensation in the water cycle. These are the ones examiners count on students to miss.

worked.stem: Describe how water from the sea ends up falling as rain.
worked.weak: The water goes up from the sea and comes down as rain.
worked.strong: Water at the sea surface gains heat energy and evaporates into water vapour. The vapour rises, cools, loses heat energy and condenses into tiny droplets, forming clouds. The droplets combine until they are heavy enough to fall as rain.
worked.whatChanged: Three stages, three marks. The weak version skips condensation, which is the stage the question exists to test.

archetypes.name: Identify and justify
archetypes.oneLine: Which one is it, and how do you know.
recognise: give a reason for your answer
state which and explain how you decided
archetypes.alwaysWants: The label, plus the one piece of evidence that decides it. The evidence is worth more than the label.
skeleton: State the identification.
Give the single decisive characteristic or observation.
If several items are listed, do this for each, and do not use the same reason twice.
archetypes.trap: Naming it correctly and giving no reason, or giving a reason that does not actually decide it. Living in water does not identify an amphibian; the change from gills to lungs does.

worked.stem: Which object is the magnet? Give a reason.
worked.weak: Object R, because it is the strongest.
worked.strong: Object R is the magnet, because it was repelled by the magnet when turned around, and only another magnet can be repelled.
worked.whatChanged: Repulsion is the only proof of a magnet. Strength and attraction do not decide it, so they cannot earn the mark.

archetypes.name: The graph or trend reading
archetypes.oneLine: Describe what the line does, then explain why it does it.
recognise: why does the graph level off
describe the shape of the graph
archetypes.alwaysWants: Two halves: a description of the trend in words, and the scientific reason for it. A flattening line almost always means a limit has been reached.
skeleton: Describe what happens first, using increases, decreases or stays constant.
Note where the behaviour changes, if it does.
Explain the reason for each part, especially the flat part.
archetypes.trap: Describing the graph and stopping. A line that levels off is the examiner asking why something has run out or reached a limit, and that is where the mark is.

worked.stem: The temperature rises, then stays at 0 degrees Celsius for several minutes, then rises again. Explain the flat part.
worked.weak: The temperature stayed the same for a while.
worked.strong: Zero degrees Celsius is the melting point of ice. During the flat part the heat energy gained is used to change the state from solid to liquid rather than to raise the temperature, so the reading stays constant until all the ice has melted.
worked.whatChanged: The weak version reads the graph aloud. The strong version says what the flat part means.
